lesson.title: What Makes a Network
lesson.summary: Introduces the computer network as a set of devices linked by shared communication paths and agreed-upon rules, explaining why both the physical link and the protocol are necessary for devices to exchange data.
lesson.body:
Imagine two computers sitting side by side with no connection between them. Each can compute, store files, and run programs on its own, but neither knows the other exists. A computer network exists to close that gap: it is a group of devices ,  computers, printers, phones, servers ,  linked together so they can send data back and forth. But a physical connection alone is not enough to make this work. If one machine sends a burst of electrical signals or radio waves and the other has no way to interpret them, that transmission is just noise. This is why every network depends on two things working together: a communication link that carries the signal, and a protocol, a shared set of rules both sides agree to follow, that tells them how to package, address, and interpret that signal. The link is the road; the protocol is the shared language and traffic rules that let travelers actually understand each other.

Think about why this pairing matters mechanically. Suppose you want to send the message "hello" from your laptop to a friend's laptop over a cable. Your computer cannot just push the letters onto the wire as-is ,  it has to break the message into a form that can travel as electrical pulses or light signals, wrap it with information about where it is going, and send it in a way the receiving computer expects. The receiving computer, following the same protocol, knows to look for that wrapping, strip it away, and reconstruct the original message. If the two machines used different rules ,  say, one expected data in fixed-size chunks and the other sent one continuous stream ,  the connection could exist physically, cable plugged in and all, and communication would still fail. This is the core reason networks are built around standardized protocols rather than ad hoc signaling: standardization lets devices built by different manufacturers, running different software, still exchange data reliably.

Scale is where this idea becomes powerful rather than just functional. Two connected laptops form the smallest possible network. Add a shared printer, and now three devices coordinate through the same link and rules, with each device using the address information in the protocol to figure out which messages are meant for it and which to ignore. Extend this same principle across a much larger space and you get a campus network: classroom desktops, dormitory laptops, library servers, and Wi-Fi access points all speaking a common protocol over a mix of cables and wireless links. A student's laptop in a dorm can send a print request that travels through several intermediate devices before reaching a printer in the library, and it works precisely because every hop along the way agrees on the same rules for addressing and formatting data, even though the physical medium changes from Wi-Fi radio waves to wired cable partway through.

This combination of shared links and shared rules is also what makes resource sharing and distributed computation possible at all. Without a network, each computer's storage, processing power, and peripherals are isolated. With one, a single printer or file server can serve hundreds of devices, and multiple machines can divide up a large computation and exchange partial results. As you move through later sections, you will see how these communication links and protocols are organized into layers, how devices are addressed uniquely, and how data actually gets moved from one machine to a specific other machine across a large, shared network ,  but the foundation is always this same pairing: something to carry the signal, and rules both ends trust to make sense of it.
